newsitem.title: INDIA: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - February 4.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - February 4.

text.p: Following is a summary of major Indian business and political stories in leading newspapers prepared for REUTERS by Business News and Information Services Pvt Ltd, New Delhi Tel:3324842, 3351006, 3761233 Fax:+91-11-3351006 Internet: biznis@giasbm01.vsnl.net.in
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
TOP STORIES
The Times Of India
PAY DISPARITY ANGERS ARMYMEN

Personnel of the armed forces were reportedly unhappy with the Fifth Pay Commission report. They felt the commission had treated them unfairly vis-a-vis the government's civilian employees. The imbalance which was being perceived, may result in the defence services voicing dissent. But to maintain the dignity and discipline of the armed forces, there would be no outright rejection of the pay panel's recommendations.
The Economic Times
TELECOM FIRMS CAN TREAT LICENCE FEE AS ASSETS

The government allowed private telecommunication firms, providing basic services, to treat the licence fee as quasi assets. Firms would now be allowed to hypothecate the licences to financiers for funding the projects. The decision also paved the way for companies to accept letters of intent and bring in the money before the end of the current fiscal. The exchequer was now assured of receiving at least 7.5 billion rupees by way of licence fee from those who had accepted the LOIs. The figure could be close to 20 billion rupees if operators of all the 22 circles agreed to accept the letters of intent.
SINGHANIA LIKELY TO HEAD AIR INDIA, INDIAN AIRLINES

Vijaypat Singhania, chairman of the Raymond's group, may take over as the new chairman of Air India and Indian Airlines. Singhania would replace Russi Modi, whose tenure ends this month as chief of the state-owned airlines. Sources said the civil aviation minister discussed Singhania's appointment with the concerned authorities and a final acceptance was expected soon. The chairman of the 5.5 billion rupee Raymond Woollen Mills and its subsidiaries has been associated with aviation since his early years.
INFRASTRUCTURE SECTOR GETS $4 BLN BORROWINGS SANCTIONS

The power, telecommunications and petroleum sectors accessed $4 billion in external commercial borrowing (ECB) sanctions in 1996/97 (April-March). This was a four-fold increase over ECB approvals sought by these sectors in the previous year. It was also nearly half the total ECBs sanctioned in the current fiscal. This year's approvals were a huge jump compared to the $0.8 billion obtained by these sectors in the previous year. Of the ECBs obtained by the infrastructure sectors, $2 billion went to the power sector and $1 billion each to telecom and petro-refinery projects. In comparison in 1995/96, the power sector was sanctioned $0.61 billion, petroleum $0.16 billion and telecommunication $32.78 million.
Financial Express
BOMBAY BOURSE PLUNGES BY 58 POINTS

Sentiments were subdued on the first day of the trading settlement at the Bombay bourse (BSE). The BSE sensitive index (Sensex) opened on a lacklustre note at 3,379.76. Further, due to continuous liquidation of long positions by bull operators, the sensex dipped to touch an intra-day low of 3,323.33 from the day's high of 3,381.72. It finally closed at 3,324.22 to register a net loss of 58.25 points or 1.72 percent over the previous close of 3,382.47 recorded on January 31, 1997. At the national bourse the index recorded a net loss of 24.45 points to close at 948.20 against the previous close of 972.65 recorded on January 31, 1997.
FOREIGN BANKS UNDERWRITE TATA-BELL LOAN

The entire loan component, amounting to nearly four billion rupees ($112.5 million), for the Tata-Bell Canada telecom joint venture was jointly underwritten by Bank of America and Toronto Dominion Bank. This was the first time banks have underwritten the foreign currency as well as the rupee funding requirements for a telecom project in the country, corporate banking sources said. The nine-year facility was contracted at 200 basis points over LIBOR, sources said. The foreign currency component in the transaction worked out to about 2.76 billion rupees ($77.5 million). The remaining 1.25 billion rupees ($35 million) was the rupee portion.
PROVIDENT FUNDS MAY BE PARKED IN DEBT INSTRUMENTS

The provident fund (PF) commission put forward a proposal to invest part of the interest accruing from the employees' PF special deposits scheme in corporate debt instruments in the capital markets. The proposal would be studied and cleared by the trustees of the commission, sources said. Once the trustees recommended the scheme, the cabinet would decide on whether to clear the scheme or not. This would be a political decision as the Left parties were not in favour of deploying employees' funds in capital markets.
STATES IN TALKS FOR ADB LOAN

Seven Indian states were negotiating with the Asian Development Bank (ADB) for various project assistance totalling over $1.6 billion. This would be the first loans to be given directly to state governments by an international funding agency. The largest tranche will go to Gujarat, which alone was looking for project assistance to the order of $600 million. The ADB was considering extending the assistance to the state governments to speed up reforms by facilitating structural adjustments at the micro-level.
Business Standard
DUNLOP INDIA CHIEF QUITS

The managing director of Dunlop India, who was recently involved in a bitter battle of attrition with the company's Dubai-based chairman and single largest shareholder M.R. Chhabria has resigned. The Dunlop board accepted the resignation with immediate effect and constituted a three member interim committee to run the day-to-day affairs of the company.
INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT BANK RESTRUCTURING TO FOCUS ON NEW
PRODUCTS

The Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI) will start restructuring by decentralising the organisational set-up, vesting more power with middle managers and bringing about greater customer focus. The restructuring was based on recommendations made by management consultants Booz Allen & Hamilton. It was aimed at positioning IDBI as a premier wholesale bank by offering a range of products such as lending and capital market advisory and risk management through an integrated group structure. The IDBI board has given an in principle approval to commence the restructuring, except in areas with regulatory and statutory implications.
STUDY TO ASSESS MULTINATIONALS' ABILITY TO COVER LOSSES

Domestic industrialists are alarmed over the financial clout of multinational companies (MNCs) that enable them to cross-subsidise, and thus sustain, continuing losses for several years in their subsidiaries. An apex industry chamber, CII, initiated a study to assess this ability of the MNCs. Faced with the inability to match the financial clout of MNCs and sustain losses over a very long period, several Indian firms expressed fears of being out-gunned in the domestic market in an increasingly globalised economy. The CII study was expected to be ready in three months and would be subsequently taken up for discussion.
CROSS-MEDIA HOLDINGS MAY BE LIMITED

The government's proposal to limit cross-media holdings may scuttle forays of print media houses into the electronic media. The Information and Broadcasting Ministry has proposed that a person or company should only be allowed to operate only one of the seven licensed electronic media services. The ministry also has proposed a 20 percent cap on equity holdings of a newspaper in a firm licensed to provide one of the services. The cabinet, however, was likely to oppose the proposals.
The Observer
INDUSTRY RECORDS 8.86 PCT GROWTH

Industrial production in the first seven months of the current fiscal (April-October 1996) indicated an overall growth of 8.86 percent. However, the rate recorded in April-September of the same year was averaging above nine percent. Despite the slowdown, several areas in the energy sector improved their performance. While production ratio in the coal sector grew by 8.3 percent, the negative growth recorded in the crude petroleum sector dipped by one percent from (-)10.3 percent noted earlier. MARGINS MAY BE WORKED OUT ON NET BASIS

The stock market regulator (SEBI) may replace the present mark-to-market system of collecting margin money on gross basis. The new system would calculate the margins to be paid by brokers on a net basis. A final decision on this was expected to be taken at the meeting of inter-bourse coordination group, convened by SEBI. The member-bourses of the IECG have been pressing for removal of the current system of mark-to-market for some time now.
REDUCED SUPPLY OF GAS TO FERTILISER PLANTS

Several fertiliser plants along the Hazira-Jagdishpur (HBJ) pipeline were paralysed following the reduced supply of gas. This resulted in daily production losses of more than $1.5 million. A section of the industry suspected an import lobby behind the cut, so that shortfall in domestic production could be made up by imports. They pointed out that industries such as steel and power were being supplied uninterrupted gas, though they could use other feedstock. However, this was denied by both the state-owned firms responsible for supplying gas. Officials attributed the cut to ongoing upgradation works on the Oil and Natural Gas Corporation's platform at Bombay.
Business Line
RATERS MANDATED FOR DIVESTMENT

The disinvestment commission, advising the government on ways to shed its stakes in state-controlled firms (PSUs), mandated CRISIL, ICRA and CARE to evaluate PSUs and pricing of their shares. The 40 PSUs, referred to the commission were divided among the credit-rating agencies. Besides valuation, the agencies were asked to spell out ways to analyse the firms, restructure a number of them as well as methods to streamline their operations.
The Hindustan Times
CALCUTTA BOOK FAIR GUTTED

A devastating fire gutted the 22nd Calcutta book fair, killing one and injuring six others. The fire raged for about three hours and took as many as 40 fire tenders to bring it under control. Except for 40 stalls, all others were destroyed to ashes in the fire. The cause of the fire was yet to be ascertained, but preliminary inquiries cited short-circuit as one of the possible reason. Sabotage was not ruled out as the fire broke out close on the heels of a demonstration by some ultra-left youth at a World Bank book stall.
